name: Laya (absorption of the mind, Kārikā 3.35, 3.42, 3.44)
description: In the Kārikā: the mind absorbed as in deep sleep (3.35), which is to be treated like desire (3.42); one should awaken the mind in laya (3.44); when the mind is neither absorbed nor distracted it is brahman (3.46).
antidotes: The text's counsel: awaken (saṃbodhayet) the mind in laya (3.44).

name: Vikṣepa (distraction in desire and enjoyment)
description: In the Kārikā: the mind distracted (vikṣipta) in desire and enjoyment (3.42), and distracted again (3.44, 3.46).
antidotes: The text's counsel: restrain it by a means (upāya) (3.42); remember that all is sorrow and turn back from desires and enjoyments (3.43); calm it again (3.44).

name: Kaṣāya (the mind "sakaṣāya", Kārikā 3.44)
description: In the Kārikā 3.44: the mind is to be known as "sakaṣāya" (having kaṣāya); when it has reached evenness it is not to be stirred.
antidotes: The text's counsel: know it (vijānīyāt); when evenness is reached do not stir it (3.44).

name: Rasāsvāda (relishing the happiness of the state)
description: In the Kārikā 3.45: one should not relish (āsvādayet) the happiness there; the word rasāsvāda for this fault is the commentators'.
antidotes: The text's counsel: be unattached (niḥsaṅga) through discernment (prajñā) (3.45).

name: The four obstacles to absorption (laya, vikṣepa, kaṣāya, rasāsvāda)
description: The four faults named by commentators for the Kārikā 3.42–3.45: laya, vikṣepa, kaṣāya, rasāsvāda; the Kārikā gives its own counsel for each.
